anchor: feeds the wound with her life-blood
title: The wound and the hidden fire (vulnus, caecus ignis)
greek: vulnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni
short: Book IV opens with the two images that govern Dido's story: love as an unhealed wound, and love as a fire burning out of sight.
body: Literally Dido 'nourishes the wound with her veins and is consumed by a hidden fire'. Page explains the double metaphor from the arrows of Love, which wound and burn at once: the wound drains her life-blood, so she is said to feed it. Conington compares 'vivit sub pectore vulnus' (4.67), the wound that 'lives' under her breast. Both images become literal as the book goes on. The wound turns into an arrow lodged in a deer's flank in the simile of 4.69-73 and finally into the sword-thrust of 4.689 (infixum stridit sub pectore vulnus); the fire becomes the pyre (4.504-5, 4.646) whose glow the Trojans see from the sea at the start of Book V. The opening At ('But the Queen') turns from Aeneas' narrative to Dido, and her wakefulness is set against the sleeping world in the night scene of 4.522ff. Students should follow the vocabulary of burning (ardet, uritur, flamma, ignis) through the book: Virgil's metaphors are a slow account of Dido's death.

title: Anna, Dido's sister (Anna soror)
greek: Anna soror
short: Dido's sister and confidante, whose advice tips her into love; Roman readers also knew her as Anna Perenna, a goddess of the Roman new year.
body: Anna is older than Virgil's poem: Servius on this line says that the early Roman poet Naevius, in his epic on the First Punic War, told whose daughters Anna and Dido were, so the pair already belonged to Roman legend. Ovid later continued her story (Fasti 3.545-656): after Dido's death Anna flees Carthage, reaches Latium, is welcomed by Aeneas, is driven out by Lavinia's jealousy, and becomes the river-nymph Anna Perenna, whose festival fell on the Ides of March. In Virgil she is the voice of practical sense. Her speech (4.31-53), which Page summarises, argues from loneliness, from the dangers surrounding the new city, and from the favour of the gods, and it 'let honour slip away' (solvitque pudorem, 4.55). Dido later blames her ('thou, O my sister, dost load me with this madness', 4.548-9), uses her as go-between with Aeneas (4.416-36), and deceives her about the pyre. Anna's lament over her dying sister (4.672-85) is the last human voice of the book.

anchor: the prints of the ancient flame
title: 'The traces of the old flame' (veteris vestigia flammae)
greek: agnosco veteris vestigia flammae
short: Dido recognises the 'tracks of the old fire', the feelings she once had for her dead husband Sychaeus. Dante gives this line to himself when Beatrice appears.
body: Vestigia are footprints or tracks: Dido means that the symptoms she feels now are those she once felt for Sychaeus. The line is the turning point of her speech. She has just admitted that Aeneas alone has swayed her and 'pushed' her tottering mind (inflexit sensus animumque labantem inpulit, 4.22-3), where Page notes that inpulit describes a decisive push to something already shaken; and she immediately counters with an oath of loyalty to the dead (4.24-9). Conington refers back to 1.719-22, where Cupid, disguised as Ascanius, begins to 'blot out Sychaeus' from her heart. The recognition is therefore double-edged: it confesses a new love and recalls the old bond she is about to break. Dante translated the line almost word for word when Beatrice appears to him in the Earthly Paradise ('conosco i segni dell'antica fiamma', Purgatorio 30.48); he turns to tell Virgil and finds him gone, so that Virgil's own words become the farewell to Virgil, and Dido's ruinous love is reversed into a saving one.

anchor: ere I soil thee, mine honour
title: Pudor: honour, shame, chastity
greek: ante, Pudor, quam te violo aut tua iura resolvo
short: Dido swears by Pudor, the personified sense of shame and marital chastity; her vow of loyalty to her dead husband is what she will break.
body: Pudor is the inner restraint that makes a person ashamed to do wrong; for a Roman woman it meant above all sexual and marital integrity. Page explains the background: Roman feeling of the stricter kind disapproved of second marriages, the epithet univira ('wife of one man') is common on tombstones, and Livy (10.23) records that only a matron married once could sacrifice to Pudicitia. Page also glosses tua iura resolvo, 'unloose thy laws', as breaking the bonds that restrain her conduct. Dido's oath is therefore a religious commitment, sealed by the image of Sychaeus keeping her love 'in the tomb' (4.28-9). The word returns at every stage: Anna's speech 'let honour slip away' (solvitque pudorem, 4.55); the narrator says Dido 'calls it marriage' to veil her fault (4.172); and on her last night she laments 'faith ill kept, that was plighted to Sychaeus' ashes' (non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo, 4.552). How severely Virgil's first readers would have judged a widow's remarriage is debated, since Augustus' own marriage laws of 18 BC actually pressed widows to remarry.

title: Iarbas, son of Ammon
greek: Iarbas; Hammone satus rapta Garamantide nympha
short: The Gaetulian king whose suit Dido refused; a son of the Libyan god Ammon, his angry prayer brings Mercury down to Carthage.
body: Iarbas belongs to the older legend of Dido. In the version preserved by Justin (18.6), cited by Conington, an African king demands Dido in marriage under threat of war, and she escapes by killing herself on a pyre, faithful to her first husband. Virgil keeps the suitor and the pyre but reverses the motive: his Dido dies because she has broken that faith. He also makes Iarbas a son of Hammon or Ammon, the ram-horned Libyan god whom Greeks identified with Zeus and Romans with Jupiter (Page on 4.198), born of a Garamantian nymph; the Garamantes lived in the Libyan interior. The parentage gives his prayer (4.206-18) its force: a pious king who has built a hundred temples asks his father whether the thunder means anything at all. His sneer at Aeneas as 'that Paris, with his effeminate crew', wearing a Maeonian (Lydian) bonnet, draws on the Roman stereotype of the soft Phrygian, as Conington and Page note on 4.215-16. Jupiter answers the barbarian's prayer at once.

title: Ceres the Law-giver (legifera Ceres); Lyaeus
greek: legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo
short: Ceres 'the law-bringer' translates the Greek Demeter Thesmophoros; with Apollo and Bacchus (Lyaeus) she is honoured before Juno, guardian of marriage.
body: Servius explains the title: Ceres is said to have invented laws, because before grain was discovered men roamed without law, and rights arose from the division of farmland; hence her Greek festival is the Thesmophoria, 'law-bringing'. Lyaeus, a title of Bacchus, he derives from the Greek lyein, 'to loosen', because wine loosens the limbs. Page offers two reasons for Dido's choice of gods: as deities of corn and wine Ceres and Bacchus belong with married love, and as bringers of civilisation they suit the founding of a city; Conington, following Henry, favours the link with marriage. Servius also records a darker ancient reading: some said these gods are hostile to marriage, Ceres because of the rape of her daughter, so that their temples and Juno's were closed to each other at Eleusis. On that reading Dido begins her prayers with the wrong powers before turning to Juno, 'guardian of the marriage bond' (cui vincla iugalia curae, 4.59). The ambiguity suits a queen whose marriage will be disputed.

title: 'Ah, ignorant minds of seers' (heu vatum ignarae mentes)
greek: heu vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant?
short: A famous ambiguous exclamation: are the seers ignorant of the future, or ignorant of Dido's love? Ancient and modern commentators disagree.
body: Dido inspects the entrails of victims, haruspicy, an Etruscan art practised at Rome, to learn the gods' will. The narrator's cry can be taken in more than one way. Servius denies that the priests are blamed for not knowing the future, since they had in fact foretold everything (compare 4.464-5); they are 'ignorant' of the queen's love, because she gave them other reasons for her sacrifices, and the cry expresses the force of a passion that no ritual can cure. Others joined vatum with ignarae, 'minds ignorant of prophecy', and Heyne thought the seers are blamed for not foreseeing Dido's terrible end. Conington keeps the ordinary construction and supports it from imitations: Apuleius' 'heu medicorum ignarae mentes' (Metamorphoses 10.2), of doctors powerless against love. Page adds that the remark is both particular and general: it applies to Dido but also states a philosophic truth about the helplessness of religion before passion, as the next words, 'what can vows or shrines do for one mad with love?', confirm.

title: Simile: the wounded deer
greek: qualis coniecta cerva sagitta... haeret lateri letalis harundo
short: Dido is a wounded doe in the Cretan woods, shot by a shepherd who does not know he has hit her; the opening wound image becomes a hunting scene.
body: A careless hind is shot from afar by a shepherd-archer who 'left the flying steel in her unaware' (nescius); she ranges through the Dictaean glades (Dicte is a Cretan mountain, and Cretan archers were proverbial) with the deadly reed clinging in her side. Page stresses nescius: the archer's ignorance answers to Aeneas' ignorance of the love he has inspired, which makes Dido's passion more pitiable; and the word order sets 'he unknowing' against 'she dying'. Macrobius thought Virgil had imitated Iliad 11.474-81, where wounded Odysseus is like a stag hit by an arrow and surrounded by jackals; Conington notes that the circumstances there are quite different. The simile reverses Book I, where Dido entered like the huntress Diana (1.498-502) and Venus met Aeneas disguised as a huntress (1.314-24). It also prepares the real hunt of 4.129-59, which ends in the cave. Wound, fire and hunt now converge in one image of a creature fleeing what is already inside her.

anchor: even as Apollo, when he leaves
title: Simile: Aeneas as Apollo leaving Lycia for Delos
greek: qualis ubi hibernam Lyciam Xanthique fluenta deserit ac Delum maternam invisit Apollo
short: Aeneas setting out for the hunt is compared to Apollo returning to Delos: a radiant pendant to Dido's comparison with Diana in Book I.
body: Apollo spent the winter at his oracle of Patara in Lycia, near the river Xanthus, and returned for the summer festival to Delos, the island where his mother Leto bore him; there Cretans, Dryopes (a people of northern Greece) and the tattooed Agathyrsi of Scythia dance at his altars, and Cynthus is the hill of Delos. Page argues that hibernam Lyciam means 'his winter home in Lycia', since a festival at Delos attended from afar implies spring or summer, and he calls the simile a pendant to that of Dido as Diana (1.498-502): the divine twins frame the doomed pair. Page and Conington both point to its model, Apollonius, Argonautica 1.307-10, where Jason setting out is compared to Apollo. The model is pointed, for Jason too was a hero helped and loved by a foreign princess and later abandoned her. The gold in Apollo's hair echoes the gold of Dido's quiver, hair and buckle a few lines earlier (4.138-9), and the arrows on his shoulder recall the archer of 4.69-73.

title: Earth and Juno Pronuba: the 'wedding' in the cave
greek: prima et Tellus et pronuba Iuno dant signum; fulsere ignes et conscius aether conubiis, summoque ulularunt vertice Nymphae
short: The union in the cave has cosmic stand-ins for a Roman wedding: Earth and Juno as matron of honour, lightning for torches, the nymphs' cry for the wedding song.
body: The pronuba was the married woman who led the bride to the marriage bed; Servius cites Varro that she had to be a woman married only once, and Juno bore the title as patron of marriage. Servius explains why Earth gives the first sign: by Etruscan lore nothing is more ill-omened for a wedding than an earthquake or a storm, and some held that Tellus presides over marriages and is invoked in their auspices. Page takes Earth and Heaven more broadly as the ancient type of all wedlock, and Conington takes prima of Earth as eldest of the gods. Each element of a wedding has its counterpart: lightning for torches, the sky as 'witness' (conscius aether), the nymphs' cry for the wedding hymn. But ululare is also used of howls of mourning, and these signs are signs of storm. Page notes that Juno's plan (4.124-5) and its fulfilment (4.165) use the same words, so that apparent accident is marked as divine design, and the narrator draws the conclusion at once: 'That day opened the gate of death.'

title: 'She calls it marriage' (coniugium vocat)
greek: coniugium vocat, hoc praetexit nomine culpam
short: The book's central ambiguity: Dido regards the union in the cave as a marriage, and Aeneas will deny that he ever made one.
body: Coniugium is the ordinary word for marriage; culpa is 'fault' or 'guilt', and praetexit means 'cloaks' or 'puts in front as a screen'. The narrator seems to judge severely, but the poem lets the question be argued. Juno had promised a real marriage (conubio iungam stabili, 4.126) and the signs of 4.166-8 imitate a wedding. Dido treats it as binding: she appeals 'by our union, by the marriage rites begun' (per conubia nostra, per inceptos hymenaeos, 4.316), and calls Aeneas 'guest' because 'that name alone remains instead of husband' (4.323-4). Aeneas answers that he 'never held out the marriage torch or entered into such a compact' (nec coniugis umquam praetendi taedas, 4.338-9), where praetendi answers the narrator's praetexit. Servius on 4.323 sums it up: Aeneas had been both guest and husband, but now denies the husband and admits only the guest. Since a Roman marriage rested on the consent of both partners rather than on one compulsory ceremony, either view could be defended, and readers have divided ever since.

title: Fama (Rumour)
greek: Fama, malum qua non aliud velocius ullum
short: Fama, 'Rumour' or 'Report', is personified as a giant winged monster, youngest sister of the Giants, covered in eyes, tongues, mouths and ears.
body: Fama means both what people say and the reputation that results, and Dido's fama will be ruined by fama. Virgil gives her a genealogy: Earth, angry with the gods after the defeat of her children, bore her as last sister to Coeus, a Titan, and Enceladus, a Giant. She begins small, grows by moving (viresque adquirit eundo), walks on the ground with her head among the clouds, and carries false and true alike. Page compares the brief personification of Rumour (Ossa) as 'messenger of Zeus' in Iliad 2.93-4, but doubts whether so elaborate a figure succeeds, since symbolic figures that try to represent many abstract qualities 'soon become grotesque'. Conington records that eighteenth-century critics disputed the passage, some finding it needlessly ambitious or overlong, and himself admires it. The figure had a long afterlife: Ovid builds her a house of echoes (Metamorphoses 12.39-63), and Rumour 'painted full of tongues' speaks the Induction to Shakespeare's 2 Henry IV. The repetition Fama... Fama (173-4) marks the moment the private union becomes public news.

title: Cyllenius: Mercury, grandson of Atlas
greek: Cyllenius; materno veniebat ab avo Cyllenia proles
short: Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia to Maia, daughter of Atlas: hence 'the Cyllenian', and hence Atlas is his 'mother's father'.
body: Mercury (Greek Hermes) was born in a cave on Cyllene, the highest mountain of Arcadia, to Maia, one of the Pleiades and a daughter of Atlas (Homeric Hymn to Hermes 1-19; Hesiod, Theogony 938-9). So when he pauses on Atlas, here the North African mountain range pictured as an old giant with snowy shoulders and an icy beard, he is resting on his grandfather (materno avo, 4.258). His equipment is Homeric: the golden sandals and the wand (virga, the caduceus) with which he leads souls up from Orcus or down to Tartarus and gives or takes away sleep. Page explains that the wand belongs to his office as psychopompos, 'escort of souls', and that the flight copies Hermes' errand to Calypso in Odyssey 5.43-54, where he too skims the waves like a seabird. Servius adds the Roman association of the caduceus with heralds of peace. The parallel with the Odyssey is pointed: in both poems a god must order a hero to leave a woman who wants to keep him.

title: Simile: Dido as a Bacchant (Thyias)
greek: qualis commotis excita sacris Thyias, ubi audito stimulant trieterica Baccho orgia nocturnusque vocat clamore Cithaeron
short: Dido raging through the city is compared to a Bacchant roused by the god's festival on Mount Cithaeron.
body: A Thyiad (Thyias) is a female worshipper of Bacchus; Servius derives the name either from Thyoneus, a title of the god, or from the Greek thyein, 'to rush madly'. Every other year (trieterica, 'every third year' by the Roman inclusive count) the sacred emblems were brought out and shaken, the cry of the god went up, and the women ran over Cithaeron, the mountain near Thebes, by night; Page and Servius explain each detail. Conington adds that the comparison is apt because queens took part in such rites, as Amata will in Book VII (7.385ff). The verb bacchatur (4.301) has already put the image into the narrative before the simile begins. The simile links Dido with the destructive maenads of Euripides' Bacchae, a link made explicit when her nightmares are compared to those of Pentheus (4.469). From here on her love is described in the language of possession and furor.

title: Hospes: 'guest' instead of 'husband'
greek: cui me moribundam deseris, hospes? hoc solum nomen quoniam de coniuge restat
short: Dido calls Aeneas hospes, 'guest', because 'husband' is the name he will not accept; the bond of guest-friendship is all she can still claim.
body: Hospes means both host and guest: someone bound to another by hospitium, the sacred, hereditary tie of guest-friendship under the protection of Jupiter, whom Dido invoked at her banquet as the god who 'gives the laws of hospitality' (1.731). She received Aeneas as a shipwrecked stranger and is now reduced to that title. Servius explains the pathos: Aeneas had been both guest and husband, but now denies the husband and admits only the guest, so that 'this name alone remains of a husband'. He adds that Virgil read these lines with great feeling when reciting privately to Augustus; (Servius says Virgil recited Books III and IV; the Life by Donatus names Books II, IV and VI.) The word frames her tragedy: at the start she was stirred by 'what guest unknown is this' (novus hospes, 4.10), and now the same word measures her loss. Betraying hospitality was the crime of Paris, which is why Iarbas' sneer at 'that Paris' (4.215) stings.

title: 'A little Aeneas' (parvulus Aeneas)
greek: si quis mihi parvulus aula luderet Aeneas, qui te tamen ore referret
short: Dido's wish for 'a little Aeneas' playing in her hall uses a diminutive, a word of everyday tenderness that epic style normally avoids.
body: Parvulus is the diminutive of parvus, 'small', a form at home in comedy, letters and love poetry and rare in the elevated diction of epic; its sudden appearance gives the most intimate moment of Dido's speech. She asks not for a dynastic heir but for a child who would 'bring back your face' (qui te tamen ore referret). Servius notices a legal undertone in mihi ('for me'): where there is no lawful marriage, children follow the mother, so the child would have been hers. The wish sharpens the contrast with Ascanius, whom Dido holds on her lap 'if so she may steal the love she may not utter' (4.84-5), and whose future kingdom is the reason Aeneas must go (4.274-6). After the speech Aeneas 'by counsel of Jove' keeps his eyes unmoved (4.331-2). Page judges that Virgil's art cannot make Aeneas look other than despicable here; others read the brevity of his reply (pauca) as the sign of feeling held down, and readers still divide.

title: Grynean Apollo (Gryneus Apollo)
greek: sed nunc Italiam magnam Gryneus Apollo, Italiam Lyciae iussere capessere sortes
short: Apollo is named from his grove and oracle at Grynium on the Aeolian coast of Asia Minor; the learned title is part of Aeneas' appeal to divine authority.
body: Page places Apollo's temple at Grynium on the coast of Aeolis; Servius locates the grove near Clazomenae and tells a local tale of Apollo and the Amazon Gryne. The 'oracles of Lycia' (Lyciae sortes) refer to Apollo's oracle at Patara (see 4.143), and Page explains sortes as oracles often written on small tablets drawn as lots. Servius observes that Aeneas had actually received his oracle at Delos (3.84-98), but here names every authority he can to show that he leaves under compulsion. The epithet is a learned one, used by Virgil of the Grynean grove in Eclogue 6.72. Dido seizes on precisely this accumulation of sanctions and throws it back with bitter repetition: 'now prophetic Apollo, now oracles of Lycia, now the very gods' interpreter sent straight from Jove' (4.376-7).

title: 'I seek Italy not of my own will' (Italiam non sponte sequor)
greek: Italiam non sponte sequor
short: Aeneas' speech ends in a half-line, 'I pursue Italy not of my own will', the hinge between personal desire and fated duty.
body: The Latin is a hemistich, one of the incomplete lines of the Aeneid. The ancient Life by Donatus says that Virgil left some lines unfinished so as not to break his momentum, calling his stop-gaps 'props' to hold up the work until solid columns came; here the break is so effective that many readers take it as deliberate. Conington explains sequor as pursuing an object that seems to retire as one advances, as in 'Italiam sequimur fugientem' (5.629). The sentence compresses Aeneas' whole case: if fate let him live by his own choice (meis auspiciis... sponte mea, 4.340-1) he would rebuild Troy, while Italy is now 'my love, my homeland' (hic amor, haec patria est, 4.347). The repeated sponte measures the distance between will and duty. Page grants the speech its formal construction but thinks Virgil knew it was an inadequate reply. The thought returns when Aeneas tells Dido's ghost, 'unwillingly, O queen, I left thy shore' (6.460).

title: Caucasus and the Hyrcanian tigers
greek: duris genuit te cautibus horrens Caucasus, Hyrcanaeque admorunt ubera tigres
short: Dido denies Aeneas a divine mother: rocks bore him and tigers nursed him. The insult reworks Patroclus' words to Achilles and Ariadne's to Theseus.
body: Caucasus is the mountain range between the Black and Caspian Seas; Hyrcania lay on the south-east shore of the Caspian and was famous for tigers. Both stand for the savage edges of the world, and Conington notes that Virgil lets Dido share his own taste for geographical names. The motif has a clear ancestry. In Iliad 16.33-5, quoted by Page, Patroclus tells Achilles that Peleus and Thetis were not his parents but the grey sea and the sheer rocks, so pitiless is his mind; Conington adds Catullus 64.154-7, where the deserted Ariadne asks what lioness bore Theseus under a lonely rock. Virgil thus casts Dido as the abandoned heroine of Catullus' poem and Aeneas, uncomfortably, as Theseus. The insult also inverts what the poem has said of its hero: he is goddess-born and of Dardanus' line, which is exactly what Dido denies (4.365). Page notes that from 4.369 she switches from 'thou' to 'he', as if arguing with herself.

title: Pius Aeneas ('good Aeneas')
greek: at pius Aeneas, quamquam lenire dolentem solando cupit... iussa tamen divum exsequitur
short: Mackail's 'good' renders pius, Aeneas' defining epithet: devoted to gods, family and country. Its placement here, after Dido collapses, is the crux of the book.
body: Pius describes dutiful devotion: to the gods, to parents and children, to one's country and the dead (see Lewis and Short, s.v.). It is Aeneas' word from his first self-introduction, 'sum pius Aeneas' (1.378), and Dido's bitterest sneer is aimed at its proofs, the man 'who, they say, carries his household's ancestral gods... who stooped his shoulders to a father outworn with age' (4.597-9). At 4.393 the epithet opens a sentence that holds both sides together: he longs to soothe her grief, groans much, is 'shaken in mind by great love' (Conington notes labefactus of the softening effect of love), and yet (tamen) carries out the gods' commands. Readers divide over the effect. Page found Aeneas' conduct in this book impossible to defend; others read his pietas as the costly subordination of private love to a public mission. The word is not ironic in itself, but Virgil sets it where its price is highest.

anchor: even as ants, mindful of winter
title: Simile: the ants
greek: ac velut ingentem formicae farris acervum cum populant hiemis memores; it nigrum campis agmen
short: The Trojans swarming to their ships are compared to ants carrying off a heap of grain: a homely, almost comic image seen through Dido's anguish.
body: Page admires these lines as worthy of the Georgics in their quiet humour and close observation, and as a deliberate contrast with the passion before them; he notes the slow, stately movement of 'it nigrum campis agmen' ('a black column advances on the plain'), a phrase said to come from Ennius, where it described elephants. Conington traces the hint to Apollonius, Argonautica 4.1452-6, where the Argonauts are compared to ants or flies, and records an old debate on whether so lowly a simile suits epic dignity, answering that Homer has similes from flies (Iliad 2.469-71, 16.641-3). The military vocabulary of agmen, 'plunder' (praedam) and the overseers who 'marshal the ranks and chastise delay' turns the insects into an army. The narrator then turns at once to the watcher on the citadel: 'What then were thy thoughts, O Dido, as thou sawest it?' The shift of scale, from tiny workers to a queen's view of the whole beach, is the point of the simile.

anchor: in full measure when I die
title: 'Heaped up by my death' (cumulatam morte remittam)
greek: quam mihi cum dederis, cumulatam morte remittam
short: Dido's message to Aeneas through Anna ends with one of the most disputed lines in Virgil; even its wording was uncertain in antiquity.
body: Conington calls this line 'the most difficult in Virgil'. The manuscripts and Servius give variants: dederis ('when you, Anna, have granted') or dederit ('when he has granted'); remittam ('I will repay') or relinquam ('I will leave'); cumulatam or cumulata. Servius reports that Virgil's literary executors, Tucca and Varius, approved dederis, and gives the sense: 'the favour you grant me heaped up, I will give up only at my death'. He records other readings: that she will crown the favour by dying, as lovers say; that she is threatening to kill Aeneas; and he wonders whether she speaks riddlingly (perplexe), as people do who are plotting harm. Mackail's 'I will restore it in full measure when I die' follows the first line of interpretation. Whatever the construction, morte ('by' or 'at death') shows that the plan of suicide is already present beneath a request for only 'a breathing-space' (tempus inane, 4.433), and Anna does not hear it.

title: Simile: the Alpine oak; 'tears fall in vain' (lacrimae volvuntur inanes)
greek: ac velut annoso validam cum robore quercum Alpini Boreae... mens immota manet, lacrimae volvuntur inanes
short: Aeneas withstands the pleas like an Alpine oak in a gale, whose roots reach as deep as its crown is high. But whose are the 'tears that fall in vain'?
body: North winds from the Alps strip the oak's leaves, but the trunk clings to the rock, its roots reaching as far towards Tartarus as its top towards heaven (4.445-6, adapted from Virgil's own Georgics 2.291-2). The simile honours Aeneas' firmness and shows that he is shaken: leaves strew the ground, 'distress thrills his mighty breast, while his purpose stays unstirred' (mens immota manet). The last half-line is famously ambiguous. Servius notes that some took the tears as Aeneas', some as Dido's, some as Anna's, and some as everyone's. Conington insists they can only be Dido's, carried and shared by Anna, and rejects Henry's view, developed from Servius' parallel between falling leaves and falling tears, that they are Aeneas' own. Many later readers have preferred Aeneas: the leaves fall from the oak as tears from the hero, while the trunk, his will, stands. The choice matters, since it decides whether Aeneas is shown as unfeeling or as suffering in silence.

title: Pentheus and Orestes: Dido as a figure of tragedy
greek: Eumenidum veluti demens videt agmina Pentheus... aut Agamemnonius scaenis agitatus Orestes
short: Dido's nightmares are compared to the madness of Pentheus and of Orestes 'driven across the stage': Virgil openly frames her as a figure of Greek tragedy.
body: Pentheus, king of Thebes, opposed the worship of Bacchus and was driven mad; one symptom, in Euripides' Bacchae 918-19, which Page quotes, is that he sees two suns and a double Thebes. Orestes, who killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge Agamemnon, is pursued by her ghost and the Furies, as in Aeschylus' Eumenides and Euripides' Orestes. Scaenis agitatus means 'hunted on the stage'; Page notes that the reading is certain and that critics have objected that Dido should be compared with the real Orestes rather than with an actor, an objection Conington answers. The effect is to make the reader see Book IV as tragedy, with its confidante, its omens and its offstage death. Both figures fit precisely. Pentheus is destroyed by Bacchus, and Dido has just been compared to a Bacchant (4.301); Orestes is hounded by a mother's curse and the avenging Dirae, whom Dido herself will invoke against Aeneas (4.610).

title: The Massylian priestess and Dido's magic rite
greek: Massylae gentis sacerdos, Hesperidum templi custos; unum exuta pedem vinclis, in veste recincta
short: Dido's pretext for the pyre is a love-spell taught by an African priestess from the garden of the Hesperides: the rite is genuine magic, its stated purpose a lie.
body: The Massyli were a people of Numidia; the Hesperides were nymphs of the far west who kept a tree of golden apples guarded by a dragon. Page explains templum as a sacred precinct (the garden rather than a temple) and the feeding of the dragon with honey and poppy as a way of keeping it on guard. The priestess's powers form the standard list of the witch: to loose or bind love, stop rivers, turn back the stars, raise ghosts. The rite draws on real magical practice: an effigy of the beloved (effigiem, 4.508), the clothes and bed he left, herbs cut by moonlight with bronze sickles, the hippomanes torn from a foal's forehead, and Dido with 'one foot unshod and garments flowing loose'. Servius explains the last detail: in a rite meant to set someone free, nothing may be tied. Page compares other signs of ritual looseness, such as unbound hair. Virgil had already written a binding love-spell in Eclogue 8.64-109. Dido protests that she arms herself with magic unwillingly (4.492-3).

title: Triple Hecate (tergemina Hecate)
greek: tergeminamque Hecaten, tria virginis ora Dianae
short: Hecate, goddess of crossroads, magic and the dead, is 'threefold': the Moon in heaven, Diana on earth, Proserpine below.
body: Page explains tergeminam as a compound meaning 'threefold', and the goddess who was Luna in heaven, Diana on earth and Hecate in the underworld as represented by a three-faced image set up where three roads met; as Hecate or the Moon she was much invoked by witches. Servius records several ancient explanations: three names according to where she is (Luna above the earth, Diana on it, Proserpina beneath it); the three phases of the moon; or three powers over birth, health and death, named Lucina, Diana and Hecate, which is why her temples stood at crossroads (hence her title Trivia, 'of the three ways'). He also notes that Hesiod made Hecate a daughter of the Titan Perses and Asteria, a separate genealogy that later poets confused. Dido calls on 'Hecate, cried on by night in crossways of cities' in her curse (4.609). In Book VI the Sibyl is priestess of 'Phoebus and Trivia' and was set over Avernus by Hecate (6.35, 6.118, 6.564-5), so the goddess links Dido's death-magic with Aeneas' descent.

title: Night: the world at rest, Dido awake
greek: nox erat et placidum carpebant fessa soporem corpora per terras
short: A calm night over the whole world is set against Dido's sleepless torment, a contrast Virgil takes from Apollonius' Medea.
body: Page draws attention to the placid rhythm of 4.522-7 and to its model in Apollonius, Argonautica 3.744-51, where night brings rest to sailors, travellers, watchmen and even a mother who has lost her children, but sleep does not come to Medea. Conington observes that Virgil is more general than his model: instead of human particulars, the whole of nature falls silent, woods, seas, stars, beasts and birds. The contrast recalls the opening of the book, where Dido is already wounded and burning with love (4.1-2). Her soliloquy (4.534-52) reviews every possible course, a Numidian marriage, following the Trojans alone or with her people, and rejects each, ending in the resolve to die and a reproach to Anna. Aeneas meanwhile 'was taking hasty sleep on his high stern' (4.554-5): the narrative cuts between the sleepless queen and the sleeping hero.

title: 'Woman is a various and changeable thing' (varium et mutabile semper femina)
greek: varium et mutabile semper femina
short: Mercury's parting gibe in Aeneas' dream puts woman in the neuter: 'a various and changeable thing, always, is woman'. It became one of Virgil's most quoted lines.
body: The grammar is contemptuous: varium and mutabile are neuter, so woman is 'a thing'. Conington compares the neuter in Eclogue 3.80, 'triste lupus stabulis' ('a wolf is a grim thing for the folds'), but notes that there no contempt is meant, while here it plainly is, and that semper generalises the sneer like the English 'men were deceivers ever'. Page quotes the French proverb 'souvent femme varie, bien fol est qui s'y fie'. The line is spoken in a dream by a figure 'in all points like to Mercury', and its purpose is to frighten Aeneas into instant flight; it is a warning of danger, not a measured verdict of the poem. Indeed the context shows the opposite of fickleness, since Dido is now 'fixed on death' (certa mori, 4.564). Students should notice who speaks the line and why before quoting it as Virgil's own opinion, as it often has been.

title: Dido's curse and the avenger from her bones (exoriare aliquis)
greek: exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor
short: Dido's curse founds the eternal enmity of Carthage and Rome and calls up an avenger from her bones; every Roman reader thought of Hannibal.
body: The curse is carefully built. Dido calls on the Sun, Juno, Hecate, the Dirae and the gods of dying Elissa, and asks that if Aeneas must reach Italy, he be harried by war, torn from Iulus, see his people die, accept an unequal peace, and 'fall before his day... unburied on a waste of sand' (4.615-20); later tradition, reported by Livy (1.2), had Aeneas die in battle by the river Numicus. Then she binds her people to hatred for all time, with no treaty between the nations. Exoriare aliquis joins a second-person verb to an indefinite pronoun, 'arise, some avenger'; Page and Conington compare the comic 'aperite aliquis' ('open up, somebody!'), here charged with wild passion. Servius says simply that she 'points to Hannibal', and Conington that the reference need hardly be pointed out. The last line, 'shore against shore, wave against water, arms against arms', is hypermetric in Latin, which Page takes as a mark of her vehemence. Myth thus becomes the cause of the Punic Wars (264-146 BC).

title: Dido's last words (vixi et quem dederat cursum Fortuna peregi)
greek: vixi et quem dederat cursum Fortuna peregi, et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago
short: Dido's last speech sums up her life like an epitaph, founder of a city and avenger of her husband, before breaking into the wish that Aeneas had never come.
body: Page admires the 'monumental simplicity and grandeur' of 4.653-6 and explains vixi as 'I have lived my life', a life complete and not empty, comparing Horace's 'vixi' (Odes 3.29.41-3). The list that follows, 'I have built a renowned city, I have seen my walls rise, I have avenged my husband', reads like a Roman funerary inscription or the record of a magistrate's achievements, and it repeats the story Venus told in Book I (1.340-68). Conington explains magna... imago as a shade both larger than life and queenly, and compares Turnus' words as he faces death (12.646-9). Only then does the speech turn to the wish 'happy, ah me! and over happy, had but the keels of Dardania never touched our shores', and her final words make her death an omen for the departing Trojans. Page notes that in pressing her lips to the couch she follows Medea in Apollonius (4.26). The two halves of the speech, public and private, are Dido's tragedy in brief.

title: Iris cuts Dido's lock: death 'before her day'
greek: nam quia nec fato, merita nec morte peribat, sed misera ante diem... hunc ego Diti sacrum iussa fero teque isto corpore solvo
short: Because Dido dies 'before her day', Proserpine has not cut the lock of hair that frees the soul; Juno sends Iris to cut it and release her.
body: Virgil explains that Dido 'perished neither by fate nor by a death she had earned, but wretchedly before her day'; Page glosses fato as death in the natural course, as opposed to a violent end. The image of the lock comes from sacrifice. Before a victim was killed, hairs were cut from its forehead and burned (as at 6.245-6), and the dying are treated as victims of the gods below. Page and Conington cite Euripides' Alcestis 73-6, where Death says he will cut the hair of the doomed queen, since the one whose hair the sword has consecrated belongs to the gods beneath the earth. Conington adds that Iris, Juno's usual messenger, here performs an office that properly belongs to Proserpine, and that he knows no precedent for it. Iris' rainbow 'athwart the sun' and the release of life 'upon the winds' close the book quietly. Those who die before their time return in the underworld (6.426-76), where Dido is found among the victims of love.
